theme: Israel’s rebellion in the wilderness; God’s mercy endures
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 106:24-48. This is the second half of the confession psalm you began on Day 97. Read it as a story that moves from rebellion to rescue, and look for the verses that describe what God does when his people forget him.
settingTheScene: On Day 97, you read the first half of this psalm, which described Israel’s failures at the Red Sea and at Horeb. Today you read the rest, which takes you through the wilderness, the entrance to the land, and the long years in Canaan. Because you have just read the crossing of the sea and the Passover, this psalm shows you what happens to a redeemed people who do not stay close to their Redeemer. It is a sober picture, and it ends with a plea.
observation: “Then they despised the pleasant land, having no faith in his promise” (v. 24). They “murmured in their tents” (v. 25).
God swore that he would cast them down in the wilderness (v. 26).
They yoked themselves to the Baal of Peor and ate sacrifices offered to the dead (v. 28).
Phinehas stood up and intervened, “and that was counted to him as righteousness from generation to generation forever” (vv. 30-31).
At the waters of Meribah, “it went ill with Moses on their account, for they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips” (vv. 32-33).
They did not destroy the peoples as the LORD commanded, but “mingled with the nations and learned to do as they did” (vv. 34-35).
They sacrificed their sons and daughters to the demons (v. 37).
The LORD “was angry with his people, and he abhorred his heritage” (v. 40), and gave them into the hand of the nations.
“Nevertheless, he looked upon their distress, when he heard their cry. For their sake he remembered his covenant, and relented according to the abundance of his steadfast love” (vv. 44-45).
“Save us, O LORD our God, and gather us from among the nations, that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise” (v. 47).
interpretation:
The second half of this psalm is harder than the first. It spans many generations, and the failure is repeated. Each generation seems to start again. The sins are the same: unbelief, idolatry, and compromise. They do not trust God’s promise of the land. They give themselves to other gods. They stop short of obedience and imitate the nations around them.

One phrase stands out: “They made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips.” Even Moses, the faithful servant, is brought down by the people’s sin. At Meribah, he struck the rock in anger, and because of it, was not allowed into the land (Numbers 20:1-13). This is a sad reminder that no human leader is perfect. Even the best of them fails. You need a greater Moses.

The story of Phinehas is one of those rare bright spots. His zeal turned away God’s anger, and the psalm says that it was “counted to him as righteousness.” The same phrase is used of Abraham in Genesis 15:6, and Paul uses it for the believer in Romans 4. The psalm presents righteousness as something credited. It is a theme that will return throughout the Bible.

The darkest verse is verse 37: they sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons. The people who had been rescued from Egypt, where Pharaoh murdered baby boys, now did the same thing to their own children. This shows how deep sin goes. Rescue from slavery does not remove the heart’s tendency to evil.

And yet the psalm does not end in despair. In verse 44, “Nevertheless.” It is one of the great words in the Bible. “He looked upon their distress, when he heard their cry. For their sake he remembered his covenant.” This is exactly what you read in Exodus 2:24. God hears, and remembers, and relents. The foundation is “the abundance of his steadfast love.” The psalm ends with a prayer for a future rescue: “Save us, O LORD our God.” This is the prayer that Israel will pray in exile, and the prayer that the church prays as we wait for the final salvation.
connection: Paul says that “these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction” (1 Corinthians 10:11). Hebrews 3 and 4 call believers not to fall as Israel did. Romans 4:3-5 quotes Genesis 15:6 on righteousness being credited. Jesus is the greater Moses, who is faithful over God’s house as a Son (Hebrews 3:5-6). The “Nevertheless” of verse 44 finds its fullest expression in Ephesians 2:4: “But God, being rich in mercy.”
application:
Be honest about where you tend to compromise. Is there a pattern of imitating the world around you? Bring it to God and ask for help.

Read Psalm 106:44-45 as a promise to yourself in your weakness. Write the word “Nevertheless” on a card.

Pray the last verse for the church, asking God to gather his scattered and discouraged people.
prayerPrompts: Confess the ways you see yourself in Israel’s drifting.
Thank God for hearing and remembering his covenant.
Ask him to gather his people and make them glad.
